'''Brent D. Mishler''' (born 1953) is an American [[Botany|botanist]] who from was the director of the [[University and Jepson Herbaria]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], from 1993 to 2023. He was also a professor in the Department of Integrative Biology, where he taught [[phylogenetics]], plant diversity, and island biology. Following his retirement in 2024 he is now Distinguished Professor Emeritus and Curator of Bryophytes, and continues an active research program.

== Early life and education ==

Mishler attended Bonita High School in La Verne, California, and worked as a Ranger-Naturalist for the Los Angeles County Nature Center Unit (Parks and Recreation Department). He received his B.S. and M.S. from [[California State Polytechnic University, Pomona]], in 1975 and 1978 respectively, then got his Ph.D. from [[Harvard University]] in 1984, working with Carroll E. Wood, [[Peter F. Stevens]] and [[Norton G. Miller]] He did his dissertation work on the systematics and evolution of the moss genus ''[[Syntrichia]]''.<ref name="CV" group="M">{{cite web |title=Brent Drennen Mishler (CV) |url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/people/Mishler_CV_July_2024.pdf |publisher=University of California, Berkeley |access-date=12 August 2022}}</ref>

== Career ==

=== Research ===

Mishler was on the faculty of the Botany Department at [[Duke University]] from 1984. He moved to the Department of Integrative Biology at [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1993.He has maintained two main areas of research: empirical studies of ecology, phylogeny, systematics, and development of mosses, and investigations into the theoretical basis of systematic and evolutionary biology. He has published over 200
scientific papers.<ref name="CV" group="M"/>

[[File:Syntrichia caninervis 01.jpg|thumb|Mishler has studied the diverse moss genus ''[[Syntrichia]]'' in the [[Pottiaceae]] family, including the desert moss ''[[Syntrichia caninervis]]''.<ref name="Bowker Stark McLetchie Mishler 2000" group="M">{{cite journal | last1=Bowker | first1=Matthew A. | last2=Stark | first2=Lloyd R. | last3=McLetchie | first3=D. Nicholas | last4=Mishler | first4=Brent D. | title=Sex expression, skewed sex ratios, and microhabitat distribution in the dioecious desert moss Syntrichia caninervis (Pottiaceae) | journal=American Journal of Botany | volume=87 | issue=4 | year=2000 | doi=10.2307/2656595 | pages=517–526| jstor=2656595 | pmid=10766723 }}</ref> ]]

Most recently, Mishler has helped to develop spatial phylogenetic tools for studying [[biodiversity]] and [[endemism]], using large-scale phylogenies and collection data in a geographic and statistical framework.<ref name="Thornhill Mishler Knerr 2016" group="M">{{cite journal |last1=Thornhill |first1=Andrew H. |last2=Mishler |first2=Brent D. |last3=Knerr |first3=Nunzio J. |last4=González-Orozco |first4=Carlos E. |last5=Costion |first5=Craig M. |last6=Crayn |first6=Darren M. |last7=Laffan |first7=Shawn W. |last8=Miller |first8=Joseph T. |title=Continental-scale spatial phylogenetics of Australian angiosperms provides insights into ecology, evolution and conservation |journal=Journal of Biogeography |volume=43 |issue=11 |date=26 May 2016 |doi=10.1111/jbi.12797 |pages=2085–2098|s2cid=89129946 }}</ref>

=== Species concept ===

Mishler has had a particular interest in [[Species#The species problem|concepts of species]] over his 40-year career, in relation to theories of biological classification in general.  He realized early on that the evolutionary processes operating in different branches of the [[Tree of life (biology)|tree of life]] are distinct enough that different criteria need to be applied to decide when lineages are diverged enough to be called species.  He later recognized that deciding which among the many nested levels in the vast tree of life should be ranked as a species is arbitrary and misleading, and began to advocate a rankless approach as was already being advocated for higher taxonomic levels by advocates of phylogenetic nomenclature in the [[PhyloCode]] naming system. Mishler argues that the species rank can and should be done away with, to be replaced by a multi-level approach to systematics, ecology, evolution, and conservation.<ref group="M">{{Citation|last=Mishler|first=Brent D.|chapter=Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics in a Post-Species World|chapter-url=https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/edit/10.1201/9780367855604-12/ecology-evolution-systematics-post-species-world-brent-mishler|title=Species Problems and Beyond|year=2022 |pages=177–190 |doi=10.1201/9780367855604-12|isbn=978-0-367-85560-4|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref> His two recent books<ref group="M">{{Cite book|last=Mishler|first=Brent D.|url=https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/oa-mono/10.1201/9781315119687/anything-species-brent-mishler|title=What, if Anything, are Species?|year=2021 |doi=10.1201/9781315119687|isbn=978-1-315-11968-7 |s2cid=233525644 }}</ref><ref group="M">Swartz, B. and B.D. Mishler (eds.). 2022 ''Speciesism in Biology and Culture: How Human Exceptionalism is Pushing Planetary Boundaries''.  Springer Nature.  {{ISBN|9783030990299}}</ref> explore this radical view of "species", and what it means for science and society to move to a rankless, phylogenetic view of biodiversity. [[Quentin D. Wheeler|Quentin Wheeler]] and Rudolf Meier note that the Mishler version of the phylogenetic species concept differs from that of Wheeler and [[Norman I. Platnick|Norman Platnick]], and that biologists like [[Ernst Mayr]] disagree with both versions.<ref name="Wheeler Meier 2000">{{cite book | last1=Wheeler | first1=Quentin D. |author1-link=Quentin D. Wheeler | last2=Meier | first2=Rudolf | title=Species concepts and phylogenetic theory : a debate | publisher=Columbia University Press | publication-place=New York | date=2000 | isbn=0-231-10142-2 | oclc=42291078 | page=x, and relevant chapters in the book}}</ref>

== Reception ==

Werner Kunz, noting that [[Charles Darwin]] "did not actually believe in the existence of species", describes Mishler as having an "extreme attitude ... related to denying any existence of biological species", shared with the botanist Konrad Bachmann, that the idea of a biological species is "worn out, hopelessly vague, or even evidently wrong".<ref name="Kunz 2013">{{cite book |last=Kunz |first=Werner |title=Do Species Exist? Principles of Taxonomic Classification |date=2013 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-3-527-66426-9 |at=2.5 The Reality of Species: Ernst Mayr vs. Charles Darwin}}</ref> The evolutionary biologist [[James Mallet]] writes that some taxonomists, including Mishler, "even argue that named [[Linnaean taxonomy|Linnean ranks]], including species, are no longer useful in taxonomy at all".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mallet |first1=James |author1-link=James Mallet |title=Encyclopedia of Biodiversity |volume=5 |date=2001 |publisher=Tarjomefa |pages=427–440 |chapter=Species, Concepts of |url=https://tarjomefa.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/4420-engilish.pdf}}</ref>

The philosopher Marco Nathan distinguishes two kinds of pluralism, heterogeneity and theory-dependence.
He defines heterogeneity as meaning that species are defined differently according to their attributes, e.g. Mayr's "interbreeding natural populations ... reproductively isolated" applies only to organisms that reproduce sexually, so asexual groups like bacteria need a different definition of species. Nathan defines theory-dependence as meaning that taxa are assigned according to the organisms being discussed and "the explanatory target at hand", so there is no unique or "natural" method for defining a species or taxa at any other level. Nathan calls the "common" labelling of heterogeneity as pluralism by biologists such as Mishler "dangerous" as it overlooks the distinction of the two kinds.<ref name="Nathan 2019">{{cite journal | last=Nathan | first=Marco J. | title=Pluralism is the Answer! What is the Question? | journal=Philosophy, Theory, and Practice in Biology | volume=11 | issue=20220112 | date=10 July 2019 | doi=10.3998/ptpbio.16039257.0011.015| s2cid=210712334 | doi-access=free | hdl=2027/spo.16039257.0011.015 | hdl-access=free }}</ref>
